mn95:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Sangha of bhikkhus, and he arrived at a brahmin village of the Kosalans called Opasāda.
mn95:1.3: There the Blessed One stayed at Opasāda, north of Opasāda, in the Devavana, the Sāla-tree Grove.
mn95:2.1: Now on that occasion the brahmin Caṅkī was living at Opasāda, a populous place with grass, wood, and water, with crops, a royal domain granted by King Pasenadi of Kosala as a royal gift, a brahmā-gift.[^1]
mn95:3.1: The brahmin householders of Opasāda heard:
mn95:3.2: “The ascetic Gotama, it seems, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from a Sakyan clan, wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Sangha of bhikkhus, has arrived at Opasāda, and is staying at Opasāda, north of Opasāda, in the Devavana, the Sāla-tree Grove.
mn95:3.3: Now a good report of that Master Gotama has been spread about thus:
mn95:3.4: ‘That Blessed One is such since he is an Arahant, fully enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.’
mn95:3.5: He declares this world with its gods, its Māras, and its Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its rulers and its people, which he has himself realized by direct knowledge.
mn95:3.6: He teaches a Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and he reveals a life divine that is utterly perfect and pure.
mn95:3.7: Now it is good to see such Arahants.”
mn95:4.1: Then the brahmin householders of Opasāda came out from Opasāda in bands, gathering in groups, and went northwards to the Devavana, the Sāla-tree Grove.
mn95:5.1: Now on that occasion the brahmin Caṅkī had gone to rest at midday on the upper terrace.
mn95:5.2: The brahmin Caṅkī saw the brahmin householders of Opasāda coming out from Opasāda in bands, gathering in groups, going northwards to the Devavana, the Sāla-tree Grove.
mn95:5.3: Seeing this, he addressed his steward:
mn95:5.4: “Why, good steward, are the brahmin householders of Opasāda coming out from Opasāda in bands, gathering in groups, and going northwards to the Devavana, the Sāla-tree Grove?”
mn95:6.1: “There is, good Caṅkī, the ascetic Gotama, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from a Sakyan clan, wandering in the Kosalan country with a large Sangha of bhikkhus, who has arrived at Opasāda, and is staying at Opasāda, north of Opasāda, in the Devavana, the Sāla-tree Grove.
mn95:6.2: Now a good report of that Master Gotama has been spread about thus:
mn95:6.3: ‘That Blessed One is such since he is an Arahant, fully enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed.’
mn95:6.4: They are going to see that Master Gotama.”
mn95:6.5: “Then, good steward, go to the brahmin householders of Opasāda, and having gone, say to them:
mn95:6.7: “Let the sirs wait, please; the brahmin Caṅkī too is going to see the ascetic Gotama.”’”
mn95:6.8: “Yes, sir,” that steward replied to the brahmin Caṅkī, and he went to the brahmin householders of Opasāda and said to them:
mn95:6.10: ‘Let the sirs wait, please; the brahmin Caṅkī too is going to see the ascetic Gotama.’”
mn95:7.1: Now on that occasion about five hundred brahmins from various provinces were staying at Opasāda for some business or other.
mn95:7.3: “The brahmin Caṅkī, it seems, is going to see the ascetic Gotama.”
mn95:7.4: Then those brahmins went to the brahmin Caṅkī and said to him:
mn95:7.5: “Is it true, as they say, that Master Caṅkī is going to see the ascetic Gotama?”
mn95:7.7: ‘I shall go to see the ascetic Gotama.’”
mn95:8.1: “Let Master Caṅkī not go to see the ascetic Gotama.
mn95:8.2: It is not proper for Master Caṅkī to go to see the ascetic Gotama;[^2]
mn95:8.3: rather it is proper for the ascetic Gotama to come to see Master Caṅkī.
mn95:8.4: For Master Caṅkī is well born on both sides, on the mother’s side and the father’s side, of pure descent seven generations back, unassailable and irreproachable in respect of birth.
mn95:8.5: Since Master Caṅkī is well born on both sides, on the mother’s side and the father’s side, of pure descent seven generations back, unassailable and irreproachable in respect of birth—on this ground it is not proper for Master Caṅkī to go to see the ascetic Gotama;
mn95:8.6: rather it is proper for the ascetic Gotama to come to see Master Caṅkī.
mn95:8.7: For Master Caṅkī is rich, with great wealth and great possessions …
mn95:8.8: for Master Caṅkī is an expert in the Three Vedas, together with their vocabularies, ritual, phonology, and etymology, and the histories as a fifth; skilled in philology and grammar, and fully versed in natural philosophy and in the marks of a great man …
mn95:8.9: for Master Caṅkī is handsome, good-looking, pleasing, possessed of supreme beauty of complexion, of divine complexion and divine appearance, no ordinary sight to see …
mn95:8.10: for Master Caṅkī is virtuous, mature in virtue, possessed of mature virtue …[^3]
mn95:8.11: for Master Caṅkī has good speech and a good delivery, possessed of urbane speech, distinct, faultless, and conveying the meaning …
mn95:8.12: for Master Caṅkī is a teacher of the teachers of many, and instructs three hundred students in the hymns …
mn95:8.13: for Master Caṅkī is honoured, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed by King Pasenadi of Kosala …
mn95:8.14: for Master Caṅkī is honoured, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed by the brahmin Pokkharasāti …
mn95:8.15: for Master Caṅkī lives at Opasāda, a populous place with grass, wood, and water, with crops, a royal domain granted by King Pasenadi of Kosala as a royal gift, a brahmā-gift.
mn95:8.16: Since Master Caṅkī lives at Opasāda, a populous place with grass, wood, and water, with crops, a royal domain granted by King Pasenadi of Kosala as a royal gift, a brahmā-gift—on this ground it is not proper for Master Caṅkī to go to see the ascetic Gotama;
mn95:8.17: rather it is proper for the ascetic Gotama to come to see Master Caṅkī.”
mn95:9.1: When this was said, the brahmin Caṅkī said to those brahmins:
mn95:9.2: “Well then, sirs, hear from me too why it is proper for us to go to see that Master Gotama;
mn95:9.3: it is not proper for that Master Gotama to come to see us.
mn95:9.4: For, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is well born on both sides, on the mother’s side and the father’s side, of pure descent seven generations back, unassailable and irreproachable in respect of birth.
mn95:9.5: Since, sirs, the ascetic Gotama is well born on both sides, on the mother’s side and the father’s side, of pure descent seven generations back, unassailable and irreproachable in respect of birth—on this ground it is not proper for that Master Gotama to come to see us;
mn95:9.6: rather it is we who should go to see that Master Gotama.
mn95:9.7: The ascetic Gotama, sirs, went forth abandoning abundant gold and silver, stored both underground and in the air …
mn95:9.8: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, while still young, a black-haired youth, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, went forth from the home life into homelessness …
mn95:9.9: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, though his mother and father wished otherwise and wept with tearful faces, shaved off his hair and beard, put on the yellow robe, and went forth from the home life into homelessness …
mn95:9.10: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, is handsome, good-looking, pleasing, possessed of supreme beauty of complexion, of divine complexion and divine appearance, no ordinary sight to see …
mn95:9.11: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, is virtuous, with noble virtue, with wholesome virtue, possessed of wholesome virtue …
mn95:9.12: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, has good speech and a good delivery, possessed of urbane speech, distinct, faultless, and conveying the meaning …
mn95:9.13: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, is a teacher of the teachers of many …
mn95:9.14: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, has exhausted lust for sensual pleasures and is rid of vacillation …[^4]
mn95:9.15: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, holds the doctrine of action, the doctrine of doing, and does not put forth what is bad for the brahmin race …[^5]
mn95:9.16: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, went forth from a high family, an unbroken noble family …
mn95:9.17: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, went forth from a rich family, of great wealth and great possessions …
mn95:9.18: people, sirs, come from foreign realms and foreign countries to question the ascetic Gotama …
mn95:9.19: many thousands of deities, sirs, have gone for refuge for life to the ascetic Gotama …[^6]
mn95:9.20: and, sirs, a good report of the ascetic Gotama has been spread about thus:
mn95:9.21: ‘That Blessed One is such since he is an Arahant, fully enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, enlightened, blessed’ …
mn95:9.22: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man …
mn95:9.23: King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, sirs, together with his sons and wives, has gone for refuge for life to the ascetic Gotama …
mn95:9.24: King Pasenadi of Kosala, sirs, together with his sons and wives, has gone for refuge for life to the ascetic Gotama …
mn95:9.25: the brahmin Pokkharasāti, sirs, together with his sons and wives, has gone for refuge for life to the ascetic Gotama …
mn95:9.26: the ascetic Gotama, sirs, has arrived at Opasāda, and is staying at Opasāda, north of Opasāda, in the Devavana, the Sāla-tree Grove.
mn95:9.27: Now whatever ascetics or brahmins come into our village territory are our guests,
mn95:9.28: and guests should be honoured, respected, revered, and venerated by us.
mn95:9.29: Since the ascetic Gotama has arrived at Opasāda, and is staying at Opasāda, north of Opasāda, in the Devavana, the Sāla-tree Grove, the ascetic Gotama is our guest,
mn95:9.30: and a guest should be honoured, respected, revered, and venerated by us.
mn95:9.31: On this ground it is not proper for that Master Gotama to come to see us;
mn95:9.32: rather it is we who should go to see that Master Gotama.
mn95:9.33: This much, sirs, is as far as I can go in praise of that Master Gotama, but that Master Gotama is not to be measured by so much praise;
mn95:9.34: that Master Gotama’s praise is immeasurable.
mn95:9.35: Even if he possessed only one of these factors, it would not be proper for that Master Gotama to come to see us;
mn95:9.36: rather it is we who should go to see that Master Gotama.
mn95:9.37: So then, sirs, let us all go to see the ascetic Gotama.”
mn95:10.1: Then the brahmin Caṅkī, together with a large group of brahmins, went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
mn95:10.2: When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side.
mn95:11.1: Now on that occasion the Blessed One was seated exchanging some pleasant conversation with very senior brahmins.
mn95:11.2: Now on that occasion there was a young student named Kāpaṭika, with a shaved head, sixteen years of age, an expert in the Three Vedas, together with their vocabularies, ritual, phonology, and etymology, and the histories as a fifth; skilled in philology and grammar, and fully versed in natural philosophy and in the marks of a great man; and he was sitting in that assembly.
mn95:11.3: While the very senior brahmins were conversing with the Blessed One, he interrupted their talk from time to time.
mn95:11.4: Then the Blessed One rebuked the student Kāpaṭika:
mn95:11.5: “Let the venerable Bhāradvāja not interrupt the very senior brahmins’ talk from time to time while they are conversing.[^7]
mn95:11.6: Let the venerable Bhāradvāja wait for the talk to finish.”
mn95:11.7: When this was said, the brahmin Caṅkī said to the Blessed One:
mn95:11.8: “Let Master Gotama not rebuke the student Kāpaṭika.
mn95:11.9: The student Kāpaṭika is of good family, he is learned, he has good delivery, he is wise, and he is capable of taking part in this discussion with Master Gotama.”
mn95:12.2: “Surely the student Kāpaṭika will have completed the threefold-knowledge tradition,
mn95:12.3: since the brahmins so honour him.”
mn95:12.4: Then it occurred to the student Kāpaṭika:
mn95:12.5: “When the ascetic Gotama turns his eyes to me, I shall ask the ascetic Gotama a question.”
mn95:12.6: Then the Blessed One, knowing the thought in the student Kāpaṭika’s mind with his own mind, turned his eyes towards the student Kāpaṭika.
mn95:12.7: Then it occurred to the student Kāpaṭika:
mn95:12.8: “The ascetic Gotama is paying attention to me.
mn95:12.9: Suppose I were to ask the ascetic Gotama a question?”
mn95:12.10: Then the student Kāpaṭika said to the Blessed One:
mn95:12.11: “Master Gotama, as to the brahmins’ ancient hymnal, handed down by oral tradition, generation after generation, coming down in the scriptures[^8]—in that matter the brahmins come to the definite conclusion:
mn95:12.12: ‘Only this is true, everything else is wrong.’[^9]
mn95:12.13: What does Master Gotama say about this?”
mn95:13.1: “How is it then, Bhāradvāja, is there even a single brahmin among the brahmins who says thus:
mn95:13.3: only this is true, everything else is wrong’?”
mn95:13.5: “How is it then, Bhāradvāja, is there even a single teacher among the brahmins, or a teacher’s teacher, or even back to the seventh generation of teachers, who says thus:
mn95:13.7: only this is true, everything else is wrong’?”
mn95:13.9: “How is it then, Bhāradvāja, did those ancient seers of the brahmins, the makers of the hymns, the composers of the hymns,[^11] whose ancient hymns, once chanted, uttered, and compiled, the brahmins nowadays still chant and repeat, repeating what has been repeated, reciting what has been recited—that is to say, Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamataggi, Aṅgirasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu—
mn95:13.12: only this is true, everything else is wrong’?”
mn95:13.14: “So then, Bhāradvāja, it seems there is not even a single brahmin among the brahmins who says thus:
mn95:13.16: only this is true, everything else is wrong’;
mn95:13.17: there is not even a single teacher among the brahmins, or a teacher’s teacher, or even back to the seventh generation of teachers, who says thus:
mn95:13.19: only this is true, everything else is wrong’;
mn95:13.20: and even those ancient seers of the brahmins, the makers of the hymns, the composers of the hymns, whose ancient hymns, once chanted, uttered, and compiled, the brahmins nowadays still chant and repeat, repeating what has been repeated, reciting what has been recited—that is to say, Aṭṭhaka, Vāmaka, Vāmadeva, Vessāmitta, Yamataggi, Aṅgirasa, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha, Kassapa, and Bhagu—even they did not say thus:
mn95:13.22: only this is true, everything else is wrong.’
mn95:13.23: Suppose, Bhāradvāja, there were a file of blind men holding on to one another—the first one does not see, the middle one does not see, and the last one does not see;
mn95:13.24: so too, Bhāradvāja, it seems to me that the brahmins’ statement turns out to be just like a file of blind men—the first one does not see, the middle one does not see, and the last one does not see.
mn95:13.26: that being so, does it not turn out that the brahmins’ faith is baseless?”
mn95:14.1: “It is not only out of faith, Master Gotama, that the brahmins honour this; the brahmins also honour it as oral tradition.”
mn95:14.2: “First, Bhāradvāja, you took your stand on faith; now you speak of oral tradition.
mn95:14.3: There are, Bhāradvāja, these five things which have a twofold result in this very life.
mn95:14.5: Faith, liking, oral tradition, reasoned reflection, and acceptance of a view after pondering it[^12]—
mn95:14.6: these, Bhāradvāja, are the five things which have a twofold result in this very life.
mn95:14.7: Now something may be firmly believed, and yet it may be hollow, empty, and false;
mn95:14.8: and something may not be firmly believed, and yet it may be factual, true, and not otherwise.
mn95:14.9: Again, something may be well liked …
mn95:14.10: something may be well transmitted by oral tradition …
mn95:14.12: something may be well pondered, and yet it may be hollow, empty, and false;
mn95:14.13: and something may not be well pondered, and yet it may be factual, true, and not otherwise.
mn95:14.14: In such a case, Bhāradvāja, it is not fitting for a wise man who safeguards truth to come to the definite conclusion:
mn95:14.15: ‘Only this is true, everything else is wrong.’”
mn95:15.1: “But, Master Gotama, in what way is there the safeguarding of truth? In what way does one safeguard truth?
mn95:15.2: We ask Master Gotama about the safeguarding of truth.”
mn95:15.3: “If a man has faith, Bhāradvāja, and he says:
mn95:15.5: in speaking thus he safeguards truth, but he does not yet come to the definite conclusion:
mn95:15.6: ‘Only this is true, everything else is wrong.’
mn95:15.7: If, Bhāradvāja, a man has a liking …
mn95:15.8: if, Bhāradvāja, a man has an oral tradition …
mn95:15.9: if, Bhāradvāja, a man has reasoned reflection …
mn95:15.10: if, Bhāradvāja, a man has acceptance of a view after pondering it,
mn95:15.11: and he says: ‘Such is my acceptance of a view after pondering it’—
mn95:15.12: in speaking thus he safeguards truth, but he does not yet come to the definite conclusion:
mn95:15.13: ‘Only this is true, everything else is wrong.’
mn95:15.14: In this way, Bhāradvāja, there is the safeguarding of truth; in this way one safeguards truth; and in this way we describe the safeguarding of truth;
mn95:15.15: but there is not yet the discovery of truth.”
mn95:16.1: “In this way, Master Gotama, there is the safeguarding of truth; in this way one safeguards truth; and we see the safeguarding of truth in this way.
mn95:16.2: But, Master Gotama, in what way is there the discovery of truth? In what way does one discover truth?
mn95:16.3: We ask Master Gotama about the discovery of truth.”
mn95:17.1: “Here, Bhāradvāja, a bhikkhu lives in dependence on some village or town.
mn95:17.2: A householder or a householder’s child approaches him and observes him with regard to three kinds of things—
mn95:17.3: things provoking greed, things provoking hate, and things provoking delusion:
mn95:17.4: ‘Are there in this venerable one any such things provoking greed, obsessed by which, with his mind possessed by them, he might, not knowing, say—
mn95:17.6: “I see”, or might urge another to act in a way that would be for that person’s harm and suffering for a long time?’
mn95:17.7: As he observes him, he comes to know thus:
mn95:17.8: ‘There are no such things provoking greed in this venerable one, obsessed by which, with his mind possessed by them, he might, not knowing, say—
mn95:17.10: “I see”, or might urge another to act in a way that would be for that person’s harm and suffering for a long time.
mn95:17.11: This venerable one’s bodily conduct and verbal conduct are such as would be expected of one who is not greedy.
mn95:17.12: And the Dhamma that this venerable one teaches is profound, hard to see, hard to discover, peaceful, sublime, unattainable by mere reasoning, subtle, to be experienced by the wise;
mn95:17.13: this Dhamma could not easily be taught by one who is greedy.’
mn95:18.1: When, observing him, he sees that he is purified of things provoking greed, he next observes him further with regard to things provoking hate:
mn95:18.2: ‘Are there in this venerable one any such things provoking hate, obsessed by which, with his mind possessed by them, he might, not knowing, say—
mn95:18.4: “I see”, or might urge another to act in a way that would be for that person’s harm and suffering for a long time?’
mn95:18.5: As he observes him, he comes to know thus:
mn95:18.6: ‘There are no such things provoking hate in this venerable one, obsessed by which, with his mind possessed by them, he might, not knowing, say—
mn95:18.8: “I see”, or might urge another to act in a way that would be for that person’s harm and suffering for a long time.
mn95:18.9: This venerable one’s bodily conduct and verbal conduct are such as would be expected of one who is not hateful.
mn95:18.10: And the Dhamma that this venerable one teaches is profound, hard to see, hard to discover, peaceful, sublime, unattainable by mere reasoning, subtle, to be experienced by the wise;
mn95:18.11: this Dhamma could not easily be taught by one who is hateful.’
mn95:19.1: When, observing him, he sees that he is purified of things provoking hate, he next observes him further with regard to things provoking delusion:
mn95:19.2: ‘Are there in this venerable one any such things provoking delusion, obsessed by which, with his mind possessed by them, he might, not knowing, say—
mn95:19.4: “I see”, or might urge another to act in a way that would be for that person’s harm and suffering for a long time?’
mn95:19.5: As he observes him, he comes to know thus:
mn95:19.6: ‘There are no such things provoking delusion in this venerable one, obsessed by which, with his mind possessed by them, he might, not knowing, say—
mn95:19.8: “I see”, or might urge another to act in a way that would be for that person’s harm and suffering for a long time.
mn95:19.9: This venerable one’s bodily conduct and verbal conduct are such as would be expected of one who is not deluded.
mn95:19.10: And the Dhamma that this venerable one teaches is profound, hard to see, hard to discover, peaceful, sublime, unattainable by mere reasoning, subtle, to be experienced by the wise;
mn95:19.11: this Dhamma could not easily be taught by one who is deluded.’
mn95:20.1: When, observing him, he sees that he is purified of things provoking delusion,
mn95:20.2: he then places his faith in him;[^13] possessed of faith, he visits him; visiting him, he pays respect; paying respect, he gives ear; giving ear, he hears the Dhamma; having heard it, he retains it; he examines the meaning of the things he has retained; when he examines the meaning, the things are accepted upon reflection; when there is acceptance upon reflection, zeal springs up; when zeal has sprung up, he applies himself; having applied himself, he weighs it up; having weighed it up, he strives; being resolute, he realizes with the body the ultimate truth and sees it, having penetrated it with wisdom.
mn95:20.3: It is to this extent, Bhāradvāja, that there is discovery of truth, to this extent that one discovers truth; and it is to this extent that we describe the discovery of truth;
mn95:20.4: but there is not yet the final arrival at truth.”
mn95:21.1: “To this extent, Master Gotama, there is discovery of truth; to this extent one discovers truth; and we see the discovery of truth to this extent.
mn95:21.2: But, Master Gotama, in what way is there the final arrival at truth? In what way does one finally arrive at truth?
mn95:21.3: We ask Master Gotama about the final arrival at truth.”
mn95:21.4: “The final arrival at truth, Bhāradvāja, is the cultivation, development, and repeated practice of those very same things.
mn95:21.5: It is to this extent, Bhāradvāja, that there is the final arrival at truth, to this extent that one finally arrives at truth; and it is to this extent that we describe the final arrival at truth.”
mn95:22.1: “To this extent, Master Gotama, there is the final arrival at truth; to this extent one finally arrives at truth; and we see the final arrival at truth to this extent.
mn95:22.2: But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for the final arrival at truth?
mn95:22.3: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for the final arrival at truth.”
mn95:22.4: “Striving, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for the final arrival at truth.
mn95:22.5: If one did not strive, one would not finally arrive at truth.
mn95:22.6: It is because one strives that one finally arrives at truth.
mn95:22.7: That is why striving is most helpful for the final arrival at truth.”
mn95:23.1: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for striving?
mn95:23.2: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for striving.”
mn95:23.3: “Weighing up, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for striving.
mn95:23.4: If one did not weigh it up, one would not strive.
mn95:23.5: It is because one weighs it up that one strives.
mn95:23.6: That is why weighing up is most helpful for striving.”
mn95:24.1: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for weighing up?
mn95:24.2: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for weighing up.”
mn95:24.3: “Application, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for weighing up.
mn95:24.4: If one did not apply oneself, one would not weigh it up.
mn95:24.5: It is because one applies oneself that one weighs it up.
mn95:24.6: That is why application is most helpful for weighing up.”
mn95:25.1: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for application?
mn95:25.2: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for application.”
mn95:25.3: “Zeal, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for application.
mn95:25.4: If zeal did not arise, one would not apply oneself.
mn95:25.5: It is because zeal arises that one applies oneself.
mn95:25.6: That is why zeal is most helpful for application.”
mn95:26.1: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for zeal?
mn95:26.2: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for zeal.”
mn95:26.3: “Acceptance of a teaching after pondering it, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for zeal.
mn95:26.4: If those teachings were not accepted upon reflection, zeal would not arise.
mn95:26.5: It is because those teachings are accepted upon reflection that zeal arises.
mn95:26.6: That is why acceptance of a teaching after pondering it is most helpful for zeal.”
mn95:27.1: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for acceptance of a teaching after pondering it?
mn95:27.2: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for acceptance of a teaching after pondering it.”
mn95:27.3: “Examination of the meaning, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for acceptance of a teaching after pondering it.
mn95:27.4: If one did not examine the meaning, those teachings would not be accepted upon reflection.
mn95:27.5: It is because one examines the meaning that those teachings are accepted upon reflection.
mn95:27.6: That is why examination of the meaning is most helpful for acceptance of a teaching after pondering it.”
mn95:28.1: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for examination of the meaning?
mn95:28.2: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for examination of the meaning.”
mn95:28.3: “Retention of the teaching,[^14] Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for examination of the meaning.
mn95:28.4: If one did not retain the teaching, one would not examine the meaning.
mn95:28.5: It is because one retains the teaching that one examines the meaning.
mn95:28.6: That is why retention of the teaching is most helpful for examination of the meaning.”
mn95:29.1: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for retention of the teaching?
mn95:29.2: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for retention of the teaching.”
mn95:29.3: “Listening to the teaching, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for retention of the teaching.
mn95:29.4: If one did not listen to the teaching, one would not retain it.
mn95:29.5: It is because one listens to the teaching that one retains it.
mn95:29.6: That is why listening to the teaching is most helpful for retention of the teaching.”
mn95:30.1: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for listening to the teaching?
mn95:30.2: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for listening to the teaching.”
mn95:30.3: “Giving ear, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for listening to the teaching.
mn95:30.4: If one did not give ear, one would not listen to the teaching.
mn95:30.5: It is because one gives ear that one listens to the teaching.
mn95:30.6: That is why giving ear is most helpful for listening to the teaching.”
mn95:31.1: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for giving ear?
mn95:31.2: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for giving ear.”
mn95:31.3: “Paying respect, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for giving ear.
mn95:31.4: If one did not pay respect, one would not give ear.
mn95:31.5: It is because one pays respect that one gives ear.
mn95:31.6: That is why paying respect is most helpful for giving ear.”
mn95:32.1: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for paying respect?
mn95:32.2: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for paying respect.”
mn95:32.3: “Visiting, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for paying respect.
mn95:32.4: If one did not visit, one would not pay respect.
mn95:32.5: It is because one visits that one pays respect.
mn95:32.6: That is why visiting is most helpful for paying respect.”
mn95:33.1: “But, Master Gotama, what thing is most helpful for visiting?
mn95:33.2: We ask Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for visiting.”
mn95:33.3: “Faith, Bhāradvāja, is most helpful for visiting.
mn95:33.4: If faith did not arise, one would not visit.
mn95:33.5: It is because faith arises that one visits.
mn95:33.6: That is why faith is most helpful for visiting.”
mn95:34.1: “We asked Master Gotama about the safeguarding of truth; Master Gotama has explained the safeguarding of truth;
mn95:34.2: and that is to our liking and satisfaction, and so we are pleased.
mn95:34.3: We asked Master Gotama about the discovery of truth; Master Gotama has explained the discovery of truth;
mn95:34.4: and that is to our liking and satisfaction, and so we are pleased.
mn95:34.5: We asked Master Gotama about the final arrival at truth; Master Gotama has explained the final arrival at truth;
mn95:34.6: and that is to our liking and satisfaction, and so we are pleased.
mn95:34.7: We asked Master Gotama about the thing most helpful for the final arrival at truth; Master Gotama has explained the thing most helpful for the final arrival at truth;
mn95:34.8: and that is to our liking and satisfaction, and so we are pleased.
mn95:34.9: And whatever we asked Master Gotama, that Master Gotama has explained;
mn95:34.10: and that is to our liking and satisfaction, and so we are pleased.
mn95:34.11: For formerly, Master Gotama, we used to think thus:
mn95:34.12: ‘Who indeed are these shaveling ascetics, menial, dark, born of the Kinsman’s foot,[^15] that they should be knowers of the Dhamma?’
mn95:34.13: But Master Gotama has aroused in me love for ascetics, confidence in ascetics, and reverence for ascetics.
mn95:35.1: Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! The Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama, as though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, holding up a lamp in the darkness for those with eyes to see forms. …
mn95:35.2: I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha. Let Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone to him for refuge from today for life.”
